turns.prompt: A job streams 10 million log records and must report the 100 with the highest latency. Why is keeping a min-heap of at most 100 latencies better than sorting all the records? In that heap, where are the smallest and the largest of the current top 100? What is the total cost of each approach?
turns.answer: Keeping a min‑heap of at most 100 entries lets us maintain only the current top‑100 while scanning the 10 million records, so we never have to store or sort the whole stream. The heap’s root (heap[0]) is the smallest latency among the current top‑100, which is the threshold a new record must exceed to be inserted; the largest latency in the top‑100 resides somewhere in the leaf nodes of the heap. Each time a record beats the root we replace it and sift‑down, which costs O(log k) with k = 100, giving an overall time of O(n log k) and only O(k) memory. By contrast, sorting all n = 10 million records costs O(n log n) time and O(n) space, which is far more expensive for this problem.

turns.prompt: An asyncio service handles many slow API calls with 'await session.get(...)'. One handler also runs a pure-Python loop that takes 3 seconds of CPU time. Explain how asyncio runs many requests at once, what happens to the other requests during that loop, and whether moving the loop into a thread would let it run on a second core in parallel with the rest.
turns.answer: Asyncio runs all of its coroutines on a single thread, and the event loop only switches between them when an `await` actually yields control, so while one request is waiting for the network the others can make progress. A pure‑Python loop that takes three seconds and never hits an `await` blocks the event loop, meaning every other pending request is frozen for the whole duration. If you move that CPU‑bound work to a separate thread (for example with `asyncio.to_thread`), the main event loop stays responsive because the thread can run while the loop continues handling I/O. However, in CPython the Global Interpreter Lock prevents true parallel execution of Python bytecode, so the threaded loop will not use a second core for Python code; you would need a process pool to get real parallelism.

grade.rationale: The candidate correctly explains single-threaded asyncio event loop switching, how a CPU-bound loop without await blocks the loop, and the limitations of threads regarding the GIL in CPython.
